refs.section_title: Heartburn; Barrett's esophagus
refs.capture: p.995 right column, entry 'Heartburn' (4 lines); p.995 left column, second entry 'Barrett's esophagus' (5 lines)

basics: The esophagus is a muscular tube from throat to stomach. Where it enters the stomach a ring of smooth muscle, the lower esophageal sphincter, stays contracted between swallows so the stomach's hydrochloric acid cannot run back up. The stomach lining survives acid because it is coated with thick alkaline mucus; the esophagus is lined by stratified squamous epithelium with no such coat. If the sphincter's resting tone is low, if abdominal pressure is high (obesity) or if the top of the stomach has slipped up through the diaphragm (hiatal hernia), acid refluxes and burns the lower esophagus. The burning felt behind the breastbone is heartburn: near the heart, nothing to do with it. Refluxed acid can also reach the larynx (laryngitis), be inhaled (cough, asthma) and dissolve tooth enamel. Alcohol, smoking, caffeine and fatty meals relax the sphincter or delay emptying. The slide omits treatment (trigger-food avoidance, H2 blockers, antacids) and the link to esophageal cancer via Barrett's change.

refs.capture: p.958 Clinical Connection box, end of its right-hand column: the final sentence 'GERD may be associated with cancer' of the esophagus

basics: A carcinoma is a cancer of epithelium, so the type depends on which lining it starts from. The esophagus is normally lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium (many layers of flat cells built to resist abrasion); cancer from it is squamous cell carcinoma. If years of acid reflux convert the lower lining into a stomach-like columnar, gland-type epithelium (Barrett's esophagus), cancer from that is adenocarcinoma. Risk factors are things that repeatedly injure or chemically insult the lining: smoke, alcohol, scalding drinks, nitrosamines from cured foods, a diet poor in protective fruit and vegetables, and anything that traps food against the wall (webs, rings, pouches, achalasia). Because the tube is narrow, a growing tumour first makes swallowing difficult (dysphagia, solids before liquids), so patients lose weight; ulcerated tumour bleeds, giving vomited blood (hematemesis). Tortora has no section on esophageal cancer; the closest material is the esophageal histology, the GERD box and the Barrett's, achalasia and dysphagia definitions.

terms.d: A malignant tumour arising from epithelial cells.

refs.capture: p.945 right column, paragraph under 'Enteric Nervous System' (start 'We first introduced you to'): location of the myenteric plexus between the muscle layers and its control of motility; Figure 24.4 below it

basics: Three structural problems of the lower esophagus. (1) The esophagus passes from chest to abdomen through a gap in the diaphragm, the esophageal hiatus. If the cardiac (top) part of the stomach slides up through that gap into the thorax it is a hiatal hernia; the diaphragm no longer helps pinch the sphincter shut, so reflux follows. (2) The gut wall has its own nerve network, the enteric nervous system; the myenteric plexus, lying between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers, times peristalsis and relaxes the lower sphincter as a swallow arrives. If its ganglion cells are destroyed the sphincter cannot relax: achalasia, with food piling up in a dilated esophagus. (3) Veins of the lower esophagus drain toward the hepatic portal vein and through the liver. When liver scarring (cirrhosis) obstructs that flow, pressure backs up and the thin submucosal veins swell into varices, silent until they rupture and bleed. The slide leaves the portal-vein mechanism unsaid.

basics: The picture shows a sliding hiatal hernia: the fundus, the rounded dome at the top of the stomach, has slid upward through the esophageal hiatus so that the esophagus–stomach junction sits in the chest rather than the abdomen. The diaphragm is a dome of skeletal muscle separating thorax from abdomen; it has three openings, for the aorta, the esophagus (with the vagus nerves) and the inferior vena cava. Normally the muscular rim of the hiatus squeezes the lower esophagus and helps the sphincter stay shut; with the stomach above it that support is lost, so reflux and heartburn follow. 'Sliding' means the junction moves up and down through the hiatus with posture and swallowing, as opposed to a rolling (para-esophageal) hernia in which the junction stays put and part of the fundus rolls up beside the esophagus, a distinction the slide does not draw. Not a Tortora figure; it is a clinical image.

refs.capture: p.944 right column, item 2 'The lamina propria' (start 'The lamina propria (lamina = thin'), the sentences on mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue; Figure 24.3 at the top of the page (label 'Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)')

basics: The stomach is a chemical hazard: it secretes hydrochloric acid (pH 1–2) and the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin. Its own wall survives only because surface cells coat it with a 1–3 mm layer of alkaline mucus and the epithelium is replaced every few days. Most bacteria die in acid, but Helicobacter pylori, a spiral, Gram-negative bacterium, survives by making urease, an enzyme that splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide; the ammonia neutralises the acid around the microbe but also damages the mucus layer and the cells beneath. Together with its proteases and the chronic inflammation it provokes (gastritis), the mucosal defence is weakened so acid and pepsin can dig ulcers. Decades of inflammation also drive cancer: adenocarcinoma of the gland-type lining, and MALT lymphoma, a tumour of the lymphoid tissue that normally sits in the lamina propria of the gut mucosa. The slide does not say that a course of antibiotics cures the infection.

basics: An ulcer is a crater where the lining has been eroded away; 'peptic' means caused by acid and pepsin. Ulcers form wherever gastric juice meets a wall whose defences have failed: most often the first part of the duodenum, which receives acid chyme from the stomach and is protected only by alkaline mucus from its duodenal (Brunner) glands, and less often the distal (pyloric) stomach. Causes: H. pylori infection, NSAIDs such as aspirin (they block protective prostaglandins), smoking. Pain, nausea and vomiting are related to meals. Complications follow the direction the crater deepens: into an artery (haemorrhage, anaemia, shock), backwards into the pancreas (pancreatitis), or straight through the wall (perforation) so that gut contents and gas escape into the peritoneal cavity, giving peritonitis and free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum). The slide lists 'weight gain': duodenal-ulcer pain is eased by food so patients eat, whereas gastric-ulcer pain is worsened by food and causes weight loss.

refs.capture: p.995 right column, entry 'Gastroscopy' (3 lines)

basics: The stomach lining is a simple columnar epithelium of mucus-secreting surface cells that dip into gastric pits and glands. Cancer of this gland-forming epithelium is an adenocarcinoma, and it most often arises in the distal part, the pyloric antrum, where H. pylori inflammation is heaviest. Chronic inflammation drives constant cell replacement and therefore mutation, which is why the book links chronic gastritis and ulcers to most stomach cancers. Nitrosamines are nitrogen compounds generated from nitrite preservatives in cured, smoked and pickled food and are DNA-damaging; blood group A is an inherited red-cell surface marker associated with modestly higher risk. Symptoms come late and are vague: weight loss, pain, anaemia from slow bleeding, and early satiety because a stiff tumour-infiltrated stomach can no longer expand to hold a meal. Diagnosis is by gastroscopy and biopsy. Tortora has no section on gastric cancer; use the stomach anatomy and histology plus the chapter 3 paragraph on inflammation and cancer.

basics: The intestines are long tubes hung from the back wall of the abdomen by double folds of peritoneum (mesentery, mesocolon) that carry their blood vessels. Whatever blocks the tube produces the same picture: contents and swallowed gas build up above the block (distension, cramping colicky pain), are forced back up (vomiting), and nothing passes below (constipation, no wind). Four mechanical causes. Hernia: a loop of bowel pushes through a weak spot in the abdominal wall inside a pouch of parietal peritoneum and can be trapped there. Adhesions: fibrous scar bands formed after surgery or peritonitis tether loops so they kink. Volvulus: a mobile loop twists around its own mesentery, kinking both the lumen and the vessels in the mesentery. Intussusception: a segment telescopes into the segment beyond it. Twisting or trapping also strangles the blood supply, so obstruction can progress to gangrene and perforation. Tortora mentions bowel obstruction only in passing; it defines hernia and the peritoneal folds.

basics: Four cartoons of mechanical obstruction. Hernia: a loop of bowel inside a peritoneal pouch bulging through a defect in the abdominal wall. Intussusception: proximal bowel telescoped inside the distal bowel. Volvulus: a loop twisted around the stalk of its mesentery. Adhesion: a scar band crossing and compressing the bowel. To anchor these to real anatomy: the peritoneum is a serous membrane with a parietal layer lining the abdominal wall and a visceral layer covering the organs; the mesentery is a fan-shaped double fold that suspends the jejunum and ileum from the posterior wall and carries their arteries and veins between its two layers. That is why a twist or a tight band cuts off blood supply as well as flow, and why obstruction quickly becomes an emergency. The groin's inguinal canal is the usual weak point for hernias, more so in males because the spermatic cord passes through it.

basics: The appendix is a blind, worm-like tube about 8 cm long hanging from the cecum in the right lower quadrant, slung by a small mesentery (the mesoappendix); its wall is packed with lymphoid tissue (MALT). Being a dead end with a narrow lumen, anything that blocks its opening traps mucus and bacteria inside: in children, swelling of the lymphoid follicles after a viral infection; in adults, a hard pellet of dried faeces (fecalith). Pressure inside rises, the blood supply in the wall is squeezed, bacteria invade and the wall inflames (appendicitis) and can die and burst within about a day. Pain begins vaguely around the navel (referred visceral pain from the midgut), then localises sharply to the right lower quadrant as the inflamed serosa rubs the parietal peritoneum. Rupture spills bacteria into the peritoneal cavity: peritonitis, which is life-threatening. Early surgical removal, now usually laparoscopic, is the treatment the slide leaves out.

basics: The gut wall has four coats: mucosa, submucosa, a muscular layer of two smooth-muscle sheets (called muscularis propria by pathologists), and serosa. A diverticulum is a pocket where the inner two coats bulge out through a weak point in the muscle coat, usually where an artery pierces it. Pockets form where pressure inside the colon is highest: the narrow sigmoid colon, especially when stools are small and hard (low-fibre diet), when a person strains, and as the wall weakens with age. Most are silent (diverticulosis). Complications: the artery beside the neck of a pocket erodes and bleeds (painless rectal bleeding); faeces lodge in a pocket and infect it (diverticulitis, with left lower abdominal pain, fever and altered bowel habit); an inflamed pocket bursts into the peritoneal cavity (perforation, peritonitis) or tunnels into a neighbouring organ, forming an abnormal channel (fistula) to bladder or vagina. A high-fibre diet bulks and softens stool, lowering pressure, which both prevents and relieves the condition.

basics: Hepatocytes normally hold a little triglyceride, burn fatty acids for ATP, make cholesterol, and package fat into lipoproteins for export to the rest of the body. When more fat reaches the liver than it can burn or ship out, as in obesity, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes and high blood lipids, triglyceride droplets accumulate inside hepatocytes: steatosis, a 'fatty liver'. Alcohol causes the same appearance; NAFLD is the label when alcohol intake is low or nil. Fat-laden hepatocytes are fragile, and in some people inflammation follows (steatohepatitis, a form of hepatitis); repeated injury and repair then replace hepatocytes with fibrous scar (cirrhosis), which raises portal pressure, ends in liver failure and raises liver-cancer risk. The book notes that cells of acinar zone 3, furthest from the incoming blood, are the first to show fat. NAFLD as such is not in Tortora; the nearest material is liver lipid metabolism, liver function tests, hepatitis and cirrhosis.

basics: Bile is made continuously by hepatocytes (about a litre a day) and, between meals, is stored in the gallbladder, which absorbs water and concentrates it up to tenfold. Bile is mostly water carrying bile salts, cholesterol, lecithin (a phospholipid), the pigment bilirubin, and ions. Cholesterol is insoluble in water; it stays in solution only while bile salts and lecithin hold it in tiny clusters (micelles). If bile carries too much cholesterol or too few bile salts, cholesterol crystallises, and the concentrating gallbladder is where crystals grow into stones (cholesterol stones). When red-cell breakdown is excessive, bilirubin pigment stones form instead. Risk rises with age; oestrogen increases cholesterol secretion into bile and slows gallbladder emptying, which explains why women, pregnancy, obesity and the contraceptive pill raise risk. Stones are often silent, but one lodging in the cystic duct or bile duct causes severe pain, obstructive jaundice or pancreatitis. Treatment is dissolving drugs, shock-wave lithotripsy or removal of the gallbladder (cholecystectomy).

basics: Red cells live about 120 days; macrophages in spleen and liver then break them down, and the iron-free ring of haem is converted to bilirubin, a yellow pigment. Bilirubin travels in blood to the liver, where hepatocytes take it up, make it water-soluble (conjugation) and secrete it into bile; in the intestine bacteria turn it into brown stercobilin (the colour of faeces) and urobilinogen, some of which reaches the urine. Posthepatic (obstructive): bile cannot drain because a gallstone or tumour blocks the ducts, so conjugated bilirubin backs into blood, giving dark urine and pale stools. basics: Each nephron filters blood through the glomerulus, a knot of capillaries, across a three-layer filtration membrane: fenestrated endothelium, a negatively charged basement membrane (repels proteins) and podocyte slit membranes (block medium-sized proteins). Normally water and small solutes pass but albumin and red cells do not. Nephrotic syndrome means the barrier has become leaky to protein without much inflammation: massive protein loss in urine lowers blood albumin, which lowers the plasma's colloid osmotic pressure, so fluid stays in the tissues (oedema); the liver responds by overproducing lipoproteins, raising blood cholesterol and lipids. Nephritic syndrome means the glomeruli are inflamed (glomerulonephritis, classically after a streptococcal throat infection): inflamed capillaries leak red cells (haematuria, 'smoky' urine) and a modest amount of protein; swelling and cell proliferation choke filtration, so nitrogenous waste accumulates in blood (azotaemia), urine output falls (oliguria) and retained salt and water raise blood pressure. 'Nephritic syndrome' as a term is not in Tortora; its features appear in the glomerulonephritis paragraph.

basics: Urine is water carrying wastes and ions close to their solubility limits. When urine is too concentrated (low water intake), too acidic or alkaline, or overloaded with one solute, crystals precipitate and grow into stones in the calyces or renal pelvis (nephrolithiasis) or lower down (urolithiasis). Calcium oxalate and phosphate stones are the majority, promoted by excess calcium and dehydration; ammonium magnesium phosphate (struvite) stones form in the alkaline urine produced by urease-making bacteria during infection; uric acid stones come from nucleic-acid breakdown; cystine stones from an inherited defect of amino-acid reabsorption. The ureter is a narrow muscular tube that propels urine by peristalsis; when it contracts hard against a lodged stone, the waves of agonising loin-to-groin pain are renal colic. Complete blockage backs urine up and balloons the renal pelvis (hydronephrosis). Large stones are shattered by shock-wave lithotripsy. basics: Tumours are named for the cell they arise from, so kidney tumours map onto kidney development and structure. The kidney forms from two embryonic tissues: metanephric mesoderm, which becomes the nephrons, and the ureteric bud, which becomes collecting ducts, calyces, renal pelvis and ureter. basics: The uterine wall has three layers: an outer serous coat (perimetrium), a thick middle coat of smooth muscle (myometrium) and the inner lining (endometrium). Fibroid cells carry oestrogen receptors, so they appear only after puberty, enlarge in pregnancy and with high oestrogen, and shrink after the menopause when oestrogen falls. Treatment ranges from nothing, to hormone-lowering drugs, to removal of the fibroids or of the uterus (hysterectomy) when symptoms demand.

basics: The ovary is built from three tissue types, and each gives its own family of tumours. (1) A single layer of simple epithelium (the ovarian mesothelium) covers the surface: surface epithelial tumours, the commonest group, grow as fluid-filled cysts and are called serous when the lining resembles the uterine tube and the fluid is thin and watery, or mucinous when the lining resembles the cervix and secretes thick mucus; they range from benign cystadenoma to cystadenocarcinoma. (2) The oocytes are germ cells: germ cell tumours, typically in young women, can differentiate into any tissue, so a mature cystic teratoma may contain skin, hair, teeth and fat, or into yolk-sac or placental tissue that secretes AFP or hCG. (3) The cortical stroma and follicle cells (granulosa and theca) are the hormone-producing sex cord–stromal component: their tumours secrete oestrogen (causing abnormal bleeding) or androgen (causing virilisation). Tortora covers ovarian histology, ovarian cysts and ovarian cancer risk factors, but not this three-way classification.

terms.d: The single cell layer covering the ovary; source of most ovarian cancers.
Producing thin, watery fluid like serum.
Producing thick mucus.
Forming a fluid-filled sac.
Oocyte lineage cell able to give rise to any tissue when it forms a tumour.
Germ cell tumour containing tissues of several types, e.g. hair, teeth, skin.
The connective-tissue framework of an organ, here the ovarian cortex around the follicles.
Embryonic cell cords that become granulosa/Sertoli and theca/Leydig cells.
Layered cells around the oocyte in a follicle that secrete oestrogens.

note: The surface-epithelial / germ-cell / sex cord–stromal classification, and serous vs mucinous tumours, are not in Tortora; the book's ovarian cancer paragraph (p.1153) lists risk factors and symptoms only.

basics: Two CT slices through the pelvis showing ovarian masses. A serous cystadenocarcinoma appears as a large, mostly fluid-density (dark) cystic mass with irregular solid parts and internal walls (septa) that brighten with contrast; it is often bilateral and accompanied by ascites, free fluid in the peritoneal cavity, because surface-epithelial tumours shed cells that seed the peritoneum. A mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) is a germ cell tumour recognisable on CT because it contains fat (very dark, like the subcutaneous fat) together with calcification or even teeth (very bright), the tissues its germ cells have differentiated into; calcification here is a reassuring sign of a benign dermoid. For orientation, find the fluid-filled bladder at the front, the uterus behind it and the rectum behind that; the ovaries normally lie to either side of the uterus. The book has no matching figure; use the ovary histology figure and the ovarian cancer paragraph.

terms.d: Malignant glandular tumour growing as a cyst.
Germ cell tumour containing mature tissues such as skin, hair, teeth and fat.
Deposition of calcium salts in tissue; very bright on X-ray and CT.
Abnormal accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity.
A partition wall inside a cyst or organ.
